article.title: Charity Begins at Home
article.author: Eva Amar
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. October is Domestic Violence Awareness Month, a time to recognize victims, honor survivors, and acknowledge the people and organizations that help them escape abuse. It is also an appropriate time to examine how organizations entrusted with protecting vulnerable people spend their resources. According to an October 13 investigation by the Los Angeles Times, 1736 Family Crisis Center, a Southern California nonprofit that receives nearly 94 percent of its revenue from government grants, provides its CEO, Carol Adelkoff, with a luxury Santa Monica apartment costing approximately $6,500 a month and a leased BMW for her use in Hawaii, where she maintains her primary residence. For an organization whose mission includes providing shelter to people who have nowhere safe to live, the arrangement presents an irony that's difficult to ignore. 1736 Family Crisis Center operates six shelters and provides counseling, legal assistance, crisis intervention, and other services. It reports serving nearly 11,000 individuals annually through direct services, including more than 4,600 children and youth. Those numbers include far more than shelter residents, but they illustrate the importance of the organization's work. Its IRS Form 990 for the fiscal year ending June 2025 reports $15,442,080 in revenue, including $14,507,714 in government grants, and $15,504,340 in expenses. The organization spent $62,260 more than it received. Those are public dollars supporting a mission that deserves public accountability. Related: Don't Look Down: America's Democracy Is Under Strain—and the World Is Watching The Women Behind the Statistics More than twenty years ago, I interviewed John Faulkner, whose 18-year-old daughter, Jessica, was murdered in May 2004 while attending the University of North Carolina Wilmington. Jessica had been stalked by Curtis Dixon, whose behavior had become increasingly threatening. Her father was left trying to understand why the warning signs had not resulted in the protection she needed. Only weeks later, another UNC Wilmington student, 22-year-old Christen Naujoks, was murdered by a former boyfriend. Christen had sought help and obtained a protective order. It wasn't enough to save her. I have carried those stories with me for more than two decades. One young woman did not know how to get the protection she needed. Another sought protection and still ended up dead. Their families were left with grief that no amount of money or public sympathy could erase. These are the women we are talking about when we discuss domestic violence. They are not simply statistics in an annual report or numbers used to justify another grant application. They are daughters, mothers, sisters, and friends whose lives may depend on whether someone answers the telephone, opens a shelter door, or recognizes the danger before it is too late. That is why organizations such as 1736 Family Crisis Center matter. And it is why their financial decisions deserve scrutiny. The People in the Trenches The staff at 1736 Family Crisis Center spend their working days trying to help save other people's lives, yet some can barely afford to support themselves. These are the people answering crisis calls, finding emergency shelter for women fleeing abusive relationships, comforting traumatized children, and sometimes making decisions that can mean the difference between life and death. They work nights, weekends, and holidays because domestic violence doesn't keep business hours. Yet residential care positions at the organization have been advertised at approximately $20 an hour, or $41,600 annually for a full-time employee before taxes. Try living on that in Los Angeles. Related: He said. He said. End of Story. In November 2022, an employee reviewing the organization on Indeed complained that the wages weren't enough to live on. That was nearly four years ago, before the cost of just about everything went up even further. And the complaints weren't limited to wages. In September 2019, an employee writing on Glassdoor questioned senior management's salaries, encouraged readers to examine the organization's IRS Form 990, and complained that the CEO rarely appeared at the office. Those are allegations from anonymous employee reviews, not independently verified findings. But it's worth considering that employees were raising questions about executive compensation and management's presence seven years before the current controversy. What Does Carol Adelkoff Actually Cost This Charity? According to the organization's IRS Form 990, Adelkoff received $816,023 in reported compensation for fiscal 2025. The previous year, she received $985,552. That's $1,801,575 over two years. Her fiscal 2025 compensation alone was equivalent to the annual earnings of nearly twenty full-time employees making $20 an hour. And we still do not know whether the apartment and vehicle benefits were included in those compensation figures or recorded separately. Meanwhile, the charity has reported operating deficits for three consecutive years: $573,097 in fiscal 2023, $172,704 in fiscal 2024, and $62,260 in fiscal 2025. That's $808,061 in cumulative deficits. Those figures do not establish that executive pay caused the shortfalls, but they do make the board's spending priorities a legitimate subject of inquiry. Then there's Ronald C. Troupe, president of the board of directors, who reportedly received $66,000 annually for approximately 30 hours of work a week. That's $24,400 more than the annual pay of a full-time employee earning $20 an hour. Related: Stay Woke: What My Father Learned About Race in America Paying a nonprofit board member is not automatically improper. But what services does Troupe provide for that money? Who approved his compensation, and how was its reasonableness determined? The board is responsible for overseeing management, not simply signing off on its decisions. Perhaps the board should consider spreading some of that generosity around. Meanwhile, Carol Adelkoff is rolling around Kamuela, on Hawaii's Big Island, in a Beemer leased by the charity. A Charity, Not a Corporation Has anyone at 1736 Family Crisis Center ever heard of the appearance of impropriety? The charity's attorney has characterized the executive apartment as a business expense rather than taxable compensation. Perhaps the arrangement is permissible under IRS rules. But legality and sound judgment are not necessarily the same thing. When nearly 94 percent of an organization's revenue comes from government grants, its board has an obligation to consider more than whether an expense can be justified on paper. It should also consider whether the expenditure is consistent with the organization's mission and the public trust placed in it. The appearance of impropriety alone should have been enough to make the board reconsider. This kind of incongruity says something about the culture of an organization and the priorities of those running it. When a charity's leadership enjoys benefits that seem so far removed from the circumstances of the people it serves, you have to wonder whether its board has lost sight of the very mission it was entrusted to protect. There are legitimate questions about how these arrangements were approved, whether personal benefits were properly accounted for, and whether the expenses were permitted under the organization's government funding agreements. Those questions deserve answers from the board and the agencies providing public money. The Cost of Losing Public Trust People support domestic-violence organizations because they want to help someone escape danger. They picture their contributions paying for a shelter bed, counseling, transportation, or basic necessities for a woman who leaves home with little more than the clothes she is wearing. They do not expect their generosity to be taken for granted. The available records do not establish which funding sources paid for the executive benefits, but that is one more reason to demand an accounting. The last thing I want is for revelations about executive compensation to discourage people from supporting an organization whose services may mean the difference between life and death. The women and families who depend on 1736 Family Crisis Center should not have to pay the price for decisions made in its executive offices. If anything, these revelations should remind us why responsible oversight is so important. The mission deserves our support, and the people entrusted with carrying it out deserve our scrutiny. There's an old saying that charity begins at home. At 1736 Family Crisis Center, someone appears to have taken that personally, and I do mean personally. Eva Amar is a community activist and contributing writer covering land use, development and government accountability in the northwest San Fernando Valley. For more than two decades, she has also advocated for campus sexual-assault victims and for legislation strengthening campus safety, transparency and accountability.
